newsitem.title: EGYPT: Small investors push Cairo bourse down - traders.
newsitem.headline: Small investors push Cairo bourse down - traders.

text.p: Egypt's bourse needs institutions to take over from inexperienced individual investors whose erratic trading habits have driven the market to six-month lows, analysts said on Thursday.
The Capital Market Authority (CMA) overall index, which rose to record highs earlier this year, has lost much of its momentum and is currently languishing at levels last seen in January.

Analysts said the downtrend, which brought the market 4.5 percent lower since July 1, was due to a natural correction exacerbated by pessimism among the small investors who entered the market en masse during its heyday.

"The small investors don't understand trends, they have no experience and they panicked during the correction. They sold because the market is low and selling made it go lower so they sold again. It's a spiral that will not be broken until the institutions are sovereign," said Mohammed Maher at analysts Prime Investments.

Analysts also say that infrastructure problems and a lack of new issues has also helped push the market deeper into the doldrums, worrying Egypt's business-oriented cabinet which is banking on the bourse to help propel the economy.

For the past week, the state has tried to remedy the downtrend, using its media to proclaim a second coming for the stock market and the privatisation programme, which is the flagship of Egypt's economic reforms.

Officials promising updated trading systems and quick settlement procedures have crowded the pages of government-owned newspapers while other articles, touting the partial privatisation of 160 public firms and maybe even a state bank, seem deliberately put there to quieten broker's complaints.
"A new plan to update the trading system in the bourse will ease the investment in securities," said a recent front-page headline in the government-owned al-Ahram daily.
Senior CMA officials have also been quoted as saying the bourse will soon scrap a five percent ceiling and floor on share prices, a measure which has irked many traders.
"The state is obviously trying to convince investors that the market is okay but that is not enough," Maher said.

Brokers say the market fundamentals are all bullish, citing price-to-earning ratios at an attractive 10 to 10.5 which is a little lower than levels during January and February when Egypt was very popular among regional markets.
Other traders are baying for foreign investors to flood the market like they did earlier this year, saying local investors will take courage from their intervention and plunge in.
They also say the foreigners want to see a more diversified market with many private firms listed alongside the equity tranches of firms in which the state had some sort of holding.
Brokers say they have faith this government will do all it can to boost the market.

"Before, we used to say the government was going on the wrong track. But now they know the way, they realise how important it is and they only have to implement it. We have confidence they will," said Mohammed Abdullah, managing director of securities house Intercapital.
